===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:moneth<alt:mon(e)th>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|moneth|mon(e)th}}, from {{inh|en|ang|mōnaþ}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*mānōþ}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*mēnōþs|t=month}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*mḗh₁n̥s|t=moon, month}}, probably derived from {{m|ine-pro|*meh₁-|t=measure}} with moon-cycles being used to measure time. Related to {{m|en|moon}}. Cognate with {{cog|stq|Mound|t=month}}, {{cog|nl|maand|t=month}}, {{cog|nds-de|Maand|t=month}}, {{cog|de|Monat|t=month}}, {{cog|da|måned|t=month}}, {{cog|sv|månad|t=month}}, {{cog|is|mánuður|t=month}}.

Eclipsed non-native {{ncog|ang|calend|t=month}}, borrowed from {{ncog|la|kalendae|calendae}}.

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[receive]], especially with a [[consent]], with [[favour]], or with [[approval]].
#* {{RQ:King James Version|book=Psalms|chapter=20|verse=3|passage=Remember all thy offerings, and '''accept''' thy burnt sacrifice.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Joseph Addison|date=1714-08-25|chapter=The Sequel of the Story of Shalum and Hilpa|title={{w|The Spectator (1711)|The Spectator}}|number=585|newversion=republished in|year2=1721|title2=The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq|volume2=4|location2=London|publisher2=Jacob Tonson|pageurl2=https://books.google.com/books?id=119Q-N9gi6MC&pg=PA112|page2=112|passage=The Chinese say, that a little time afterwards she '''accepted''' of a treat in one of the neighbouring hills to which Shalum had invited her.}}
#* {{RQ:Bulwer-Lytton Zanoni|volume=I|chapter=III|page=151|passage=I bid thee banish from thy heart all thought of me, but as one whom the Future cries aloud to thee to avoid. Glyndon, if thou '''acceptest''' his homage, will love thee till the tomb closes upon both.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[take up]] something [[given]], or [[submit]] to something [[imposed]], either [[willingly]] or [[reluctantly]].
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[admit]] to a place or a group.
#: {{ux|en|The Boy Scouts were going to '''accept''' him as a member.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To regard as proper, usual, true, or to believe in.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' the notion that Christ lived.}}
#: {{ux|en|I can't '''accept''' nothing being done about the problem and your standing idly by.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive as adequate or satisfactory.
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive or [[admit]] to; to [[agree]] to; to [[assent]] to; to [[submit]] to.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' your proposal, amendment, or excuse.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[endure]] patiently.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' my punishment.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To acknowledge patiently without [[opposition]] or [[resistance]].
#: {{ux|en|We need to '''accept''' the fact that restaurants are closed due to COVID-19 and that no amount of wishing or screaming will make them reopen any sooner.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|legal|business}} To agree to pay.
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive [[officially]].
#: {{co|en|to '''accept''' the report of a committee}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To receive something willingly.
# {{lb|en|Philippines}} To do a service done by an establishment.
#: {{ux|en|We '''accept''' repairs.}}
#: {{ux|en|We '''accept''' bookbinding.}}

====Usage notes====
* In senses 1.1, 1.3, and 1.4, the plural is most commonly ''people''. In senses 1.2, 2, 3, and 5, ''persons'' is the only plural.
* Traditionally a distinction was often made in formal language whereby ''people'' was used of human beings in general and of larger, more anonymous groups, while ''persons'' described a finite, known number of individuals. To the degree that speakers still use the plural ''persons'', it is indeed often restricted to this latter context. However, Garner considers the distinction pedantic and most style guides (including e.g. the Associated Press and New York Times) now recommend ''people''. ''Persons'' is still generally used in technical and legal contexts.
* Referring to an individual as a “person” (rather than a gentleman, lady, etc.) was formerly perceived as a slight:
: '''1836''', {{w|William IV of the United Kingdom|King William IV}}, quoted in Clare Jerrold, ''[https://archive.org/stream/earlycourtofquee00jerruoft/earlycourtofquee00jerruoft_djvu.txt The Early Court of Queen Victoria]'' (New York: Putnam, 1912), at p. 97:
:: I trust in God that my life may be spared for nine months longer, after which period, in the event of my death, no Regency would take place. I should then have the satisfaction of leaving the Royal authority to the personal exercise of that young lady [the future Queen Victoria], the heiress presumptive to the Crown, and not in the hands of a '''person''' now near me [Victoria's mother], who is surrounded by evil advisers and who is herself incompetent to act with propriety in the station in which she would be placed. I have no hesitation in saying that I have been insulted, grossly insulted by that '''person,''' but I am determined to endure no longer a course of behaviour so disrespectful to me.

Displaced native {{ncog|enm|he}} from {{ncog|ang|hīe}} — which vowel changes had left indistinct from {{m|enm|he|t=he}} — by the 1400s,{{R:Etymonline}}Otto Jespersen, ''Growth and Structure of the English Language'' being readily incorporated alongside native words beginning with the same sound ({{m|en|the}}, {{m|en|that}}, {{m|en|this}}). Used as a singular pronoun since 1300, e.g. in the 1325 ''Cursor Mundi''. The Norse term (whence also {{cog|is|þeir|t=they}}, {{cog|fo|teir|t=they}}, {{cog|da|de|t=they}}, {{cog|sv|de|t=they}}, {{cog|nn|dei|t=they}}) is from {{der|en|gem-pro|*þai|t=those}} (from {{der|en|ine-pro|*só|*to-|that}}), whence also {{cog|ang|þā|t=those}} (whence obsolete English {{dbt|en|tho|notext=1}}), {{cog|sco|thae}}, {{m|sco|thai}}, {{m|sco|thay|t=they; those}}, {{cog|swg|dia|t=they}}. The origin of the determiner {{m|en|they|t=the, those}} is unclear. The ''OED'', ''English Dialect Dictionary'' and ''Middle English Dictionary''{{R:MED Online|entry=thei|pos=pron|id=MED45106|accessdate=2016-01-28}} define it and its Middle English predecessor {{m|enm|thei}} as a demonstrative determiner or adjective meaning “those” or “the”. This could be a continuation of the use of the English pronoun {{m|en|they}}'s Old Norse etymon {{m|non|þeir}} as a demonstrative meaning “those”, but the ''OED'' and ''EDD'' say it is limited to southern, especially southwestern, England, specifically outside the region of Norse contact. ====Pronoun==== {{en-pron|desc=third-person, nominative case, usually plural, sometimes singular|objective case|them|possessive|their|possessive noun|theirs|reflexive|themselves|or reflexive singular|themself}} # {{senseid|en|third-person plural nominative}} {{lb|en|the third-person plural nominative}} A group of entities previously mentioned. {{defdate|since 13th c.}} #: {{ux|en|Fred and Jane? That's just what '''they''' want you to think.}} # {{lb|en|bridge}} The opponents of the side which is [[keep score|keeping score]]. #: {{ant|en|we}} =====Usage notes===== * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Usage of ''they'' as a singular pronoun began in the 1300s and has been common ever since, despite attempts by some grammarians, beginning in 1795,Anne Bodine, ''Androcentrism in Prescriptive Grammar: Singular 'they', Sex-indefinite 'he', and 'he or she''', in ''Language in Society'', v. 4 (1975), pages 129–146 to condemn it as a violation of traditional ([[Latinate]]) agreement rules. Some other grammarians have countered that criticism since at least 1896.William Malone Baskervill and James Witt Sewell's ''An English Grammar'' (1896) says singular ''they'' is "frequently found ''when the antecedent includes or implies both genders''. The masculine does not really represent a feminine antecedent"; it furthermore recommends changing it to ''he'' or ''she'' "''unless both genders are implied''". (Italics in original.) ''Fowler's Modern English Usage'' (third edition) notes that it "is being left unaltered by copy editors" and is "not widely felt to lie in a prohibited zone". Some authors compare use of singular ''they'' to widespread use of singular ''you'' instead of ''thou''.Michael Reed, ''Tech Book 1'' {{ISBN|0956081312}}, ''Note about pronoun usage'', page 9: "Singular ''they'' can introduce some ambiguity because the antecedent of the pronoun “they” could theoretically be a male or female [... but] English has survived the loss of pronouns such as ''thou'' (singular ''you'') despite the consequent potential for ambiguity."John McWhorter, ''Word on the Street: Debunking the Myth of a Pure Standard'' (2009, {{ISBN|0786731478}}: "In this light, our modern grammarians' discomfort with singular ''they'' is nothing but this comical intermediate stage in an inevitable change, as misguided and futile as the old grumbles about singular ''you''." See {{w|singular they|Wikipedia's article on singular ''they''}} for more; see also the usage notes about {{m|en|themself}}. (Compare {{m|en|he}}.) * {{sense|singular pronoun}} In the past, ''they'' tended to be used of a generic or unidentified person, or someone who was not previously named or identified as male or female. It has increasingly been used to refer to an unnamed person even if the gender of the person is known. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Even when used as a singular pronoun, in standard English singular ''they'' uses the same verb conjugations as plural ''they'', like singular and plural ''you'': "George, you ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} here when the masked figure ran past, ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} they wearing red or blue?" * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual person of known, binary gender. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single person of specified sex or gender|citations]]. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual animal which would more commonly be referred to as ''[[it]]''. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single animal or plant|citations]]. * {{sense|indefinite pronoun}} ''[[one|One]]'' is also an indefinite pronoun, but the two words do not mean the same thing and are rarely interchangeable. "They" refers to people in general (hence the expressions {{m|en|they say}}, {{m|en|so they say}}, {{m|en|you know what they say}}), whereas "one" refers to one person (often such that what is true for that person is true for everyone). ''You'' may also be used to refer to people in general; such use of that pronoun is called the [[generic you#Noun|generic ''you'']]. *: ''They say beauty is in the eye of the beholder.'' *: ''One may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' *: ''You may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' =====Alternative forms===== * {{alt|en|They}} {{q|honorific}} * {{alt|en|dey}} {{root|en|ine-pro|*(s)tewp-}}
{{ety|en|id=cease moving|:inh|enm:stoppen}}
From {{inh|en|enm|stoppen}}, {{m|enm|stoppien}}, from {{inh|en|ang|stoppian|t=to stop, close}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*stoppōn}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*stuppōną|t=to stop, close}}, {{m|gem-pro|*stuppijaną|t=to push, pierce, prick}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*(s)tewp-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*(s)tewb-|t=to push; stick}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*(s)tew-|t=to bump; impact; butt; push; beat; strike; hit}}.

Cognate with {{cog|stq|stopje||to stop, block}}, {{cog|fy|stopje||to stop}}, {{cog|nl|stoppen||to stop}}, {{cog|nds|stoppen||to stop}}, {{cog|de|stopfen||to be filling, stuff}}, {{cog|de|stoppen||to stop}}, {{cog|da,nb|stoppe||to stop}}, {{cog|is,nn,sv|stoppa||to stop}}, {{cog|gmh|stupfen}}, {{m|gmh|stüpfen||to pierce}}. More at [[stuff]], [[stump]].

Alternative etymology derives Proto-West Germanic *''stoppōn'' from an assumed {{cog|la-vul|*stūpāre}}, {{m|la|*stuppāre||to stop up with tow}}, from {{m|la|stūpa}}, {{m|la|stīpa}}, {{m|la|stuppa||tow, flax, oakum}}, from {{cog|grc|στύπη}}, {{m|grc|στύππη||tow, flax, oakum}}. This derivation, however, is doubtful, as the earliest instances of the Germanic verb do not carry the meaning of "stuff, stop with tow". Rather, these senses developed later in response to influence from similar sounding words in Latin and Romance.<ref>The Century Dictionary and Cyclopedia, "stop".</ref>

=====Usage notes=====
* This is a [[catenative verb]] that takes the ''gerund [[-ing]]'' to indicate the ending action (''stop thinking''), or the ''to'' infinitive to indicate the purpose of the interruption (''stop to think''). See [[Appendix:English_catenative_verbs#Difference_in_meaning|Appendix:English catenative verbs]] for more information.
* When used causatively, the verb can either be followed directly by its dependent clause (for example, ''to stop them exploding'') or take a helper word, usually ''[[from]]'', before the clause (''to stop them from exploding'').  The former usage is more common in Britain, and the latter usage  more common in America.

|passage=It is a great step toward the mastery of our desires to give this '''stop''' to them.}}

|passage=So melancholy a prospect should inspire us with zeal to oppose some '''stop''' to the rising torrent.}}

## {{lb|en|engineering}} A device, or piece, as a pin, block, pawl, etc., for arresting or limiting motion, or for determining the position to which another part shall be brought.
## {{lb|en|architecture}} A member, plain or moulded, formed of a separate piece and fixed to a jamb, against which a door or window shuts.

# A symbol used for purposes of punctuation and representing a pause or separating clauses, particularly a [[full stop]], [[comma]], [[colon]] or [[semicolon]].

#: {{ux|en|The organ is loudest when all the '''stops''' are pulled.}}
# {{lb|en|music}} One of the vent-holes in a [[wind instrument]], or the place on the wire of a [[stringed instrument]], by the stopping or pressing of which certain notes are produced.
# {{lb|en|tennis}} A very [[short]] [[shot]] which touches the ground close behind the [[net]] and is intended to bounce as little as possible.
# {{lb|en|football}} A [[save]]; preventing the opposition from scoring a goal.
# {{lb|en|zoology}} The [[depression]] in a dog’s face between the skull and the nasal bones.
#: {{ux|en|The '''stop''' in a bulldog's face is very marked.}}
# A marking on a rabbit's hind foot.
#: {{ux|en|The American Rabbit Breeders Association holds that the '''stops''' of a [[Dutch rabbit]] should be white from the toes to one third of the way along the foot.}}
# {{lb|en|photography}} A part of a [[photographic]] system that reduces the amount of [[light]].
# {{lb|en|photography}} A unit of [[exposure]] corresponding to a doubling of the [[brightness]] of an image.
# {{lb|en|photography}} An [[f-stop]].
# The [[diaphragm]] used in optical instruments to cut off the marginal portions of a beam of light passing through lenses.
# {{lb|en|fencing}} A [[coup d'arret]], or [[stop thrust]].
# {{lb|en|UK|grammar|informal}} {{ellipsis of|en|full stop}}.

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|arriven}}, {{m|enm|ariven}}, from {{der|en|fro|ariver}}, from {{der|en|la-eme|adripo|adrīpāre|t=to land, come ashore}}, derived from {{der|en|la|rīpa|t=shore, river-bank}}. Displaced native {{m|en|oncome}}, {{m|sco|tocome}}.

For the semantic evolution, compare {{cog|ang|ġelandian}}, {{m|ang|ġelendan}}, {{m|ang|lendan|t=to arrive at land; land}} > Middle English {{m|enm|alenden}}, {{m|enm|landen|t=to arrive; arrive at shore; land}}.

===Etymology 1===
From {{inh|en|enm|limit}}, from {{der|en|fro|limit}}, from oblique stem of {{der|en|la|līmes|alt=līmes, līmit-||a cross-path or balk between fields, hence a boundary, boundary line or wall, any path or road, border, limit}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|ġemǣre}}. {{doublet|en|limes}}.

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# A restriction; a [[bound]] beyond which one may not [[go]] or [[proceed]].
#: {{ux|en|There are several existing '''limits''' to executive power.}}
#: {{ux|en|Two drinks is my '''limit''' tonight.}}
#* {{RQ:Dickens Nicholas Nickleby|chapter=21|text=It is the conductor which communicates to the inhabitants of regions beyond its '''limit''' {{...}}}}
#* {{RQ:Joyce Ulysses|chapter=Episode 17|passage=Ever he would wander, selfcompelled, to the extreme '''limit''' of his cometary orbit, beyond the fixed stars and variable suns and telescopic planets, astronomical waifs and strays, to the extreme boundary of space {{...}}}}
# {{lb|en|mathematics}} A value to which a [[sequence]] [[converge]]s. Equivalently, the common value of the [[upper limit]] and the [[lower limit]] of a sequence: if the upper and lower limits are different, then the sequence has no limit (i.e., does not converge).
#: {{ux|en|The sequence of reciprocals has zero as its '''limit'''.}}
# {{lb|en|mathematics}} Any of several abstractions of this concept of limit.
#: {{ux|en|Category theory defines a very general concept of '''limit'''.}}
# {{lb|en|category theory}} The [[cone]] of a [[diagram]] [[factor through|through]] which any other cone of that same diagram can [[factor through|factor]] uniquely.
#: {{synonyms|en|inverse limit|projective limit}}
#: {{hyponyms|en|terminal object|categorical product|pullback|equalizer|identity morphism}}
# {{lb|en|poker}} [[fixed limit|Fixed limit]].
# The [[final]], [[utmost]], or [[furthest]] [[point]]; the border or edge.
#: {{ux|en|the '''limit''' of a walk, of a town, or of a country}}
#* {{RQ:Pope Windsor Forest|passage=As eager of the chase, the maid / Beyond the forest's verdant '''limits''' strayed.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} The space or thing defined by limits.
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Henry 4-1|III|i|passage=The archdeacon hath divided it / Into three '''limits''' very equally.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} That [[terminate]]s a [[period of time]]; hence, the [[period]] itself; the [[full]] [[time]] or [[extent]].
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Richard 2|I|iii|passage=the dateless '''limit''' of thy dear exile}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Richard 3|III|iii|passage=The '''limit''' of your lives is out.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A restriction; a check or curb; a hindrance.
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Henry 6-3|II|ii|passage=I prithee, give no '''limits''' to my tongue.}}
# {{lb|en|logic|metaphysics}} A determining feature; a distinguishing characteristic.
# {{lb|en|cycling}} The first group of riders to depart in a [[handicap]] race.
# {{lb|en|colloquial|as "the limit"}} A person who is [[exasperating]], [[intolerable]], [[astounding]], etc.
# {{lb|en|music}} {{ellipsis of|en|harmonic limit}}.
